newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU agrees in principle to no new taxes on Internet.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees in principle to no new taxes on Internet.

text.p: A European Union-sponsored conference on Internet commerce agreed in principle on Tuesday there would be no new trade barriers or taxes imposed on companies or individuals wishing to do business in cyberspace.

While the conference, attended by 40 government ministers from Europe, the United States, Japan and Canada, embraced some ideas U.S. President Bill Clinton proposed last week, it stopped short of advocating the U.S. proposal in full.

In a joint declaration at the end of the two-day event, they said Internet regulation should be market-led but appeared to make little progress on how to regulate encryption technology needed to conduct secure transactions on the Internet.
"Ministers support the principle of non-discriminatory taxes on the use of Global Information Networks," they said in the so-called Bonn Declaration.
But they vowed to make a concerted effort to clamp down on tax evasion on business deals conducted on the Internet.

"They (ministers) agree that tax issues of electronic commerce call for international cooperation and where appropriate, coordination in order to avoid distortion of competition," the declaration said.
Clinton had proposed to create a "free-trade zone" on the Internet. He wanted an agreement on this within a year within the context of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
The document was signed by a total of 29 countries, including all EU members, Eastern European nations and members of the European Free Trade Association.
The United States, Canada, Japan and Russia were observers at the conference and did not sign the final statement.
U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley brought Clinton's proposal to the conference, but the ministers did not mention it in their declaration of intent on the issue.
The ministers identified data security and cryptography use as key issues and vowed to work towards making strong encryption technology available for electronic commerce.

"Ministers strongly encourage industry to promote the development of secure technologies for information and communication systems," the declaraion said, pointing to Europe's Organisation for Economic Coooperation and Development (OECD) guidelines.

They said their governments would promote a free flow of information on global information highways and would consult industry on types of regulatory measures needed on the Internet rather than taking up the matter themselves.
The private sector had a key role in developing global information networks, they said.

"Ministers will cooperate with the OECD, WTO and other institutions to identify and dismantle obstacles to the use of electronic commerce, to prevent the establishment of new barriers and establish a clear, predictable legal framework.

"Ministers consider that the expansion of Global Information Networks must essentially be market-led and left to private initiative...in partiucular, that private enterprise should drive the expansion of electronic commerce in Europe," the statement said.
